claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength despite favorable ductility and machinability.
The relatively low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi are governed by low effective lattice distortion.
The relatively low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi are also governed by an absence of intrinsic nanoscale obstacles such as fine precipitates or strengthening grain-boundary structures.
A simple single-phase CoCrFeNiTi solid solution provides little inherent solid-solution or precipitation strengthening.
Weak solid-solution and precipitation strengthening facilitate easy dislocation glide and thereby favorable plasticity and machinability.
The constituent atomic sizes in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are sufficiently balanced to produce only modest lattice distortion.
Substituting approximately 3–5 at% with an element selected for atomic-size mismatch will increase local lattice distortion.
A minor atomic-size-mismatched alloying addition can promote nanoscale precipitation.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can refine grains and promote fine precipitate formation in the proposed alloy.
Nanoscale precipitates and grain-boundary structures impede dislocation motion.
Increasing lattice mismatch and producing strengthening heterogeneities will increase the hardness and compressive strength of CoCrFeNiTi relative to the baseline alloy.
The predicted increase in hardness and compressive strength will likely be accompanied by reduced plasticity.
The initial material can be prepared as a homogeneous single BCC or FCC/BCC solid-solution microstructure by standard melting and solution annealing.
The proposed mechanism applies from approximately 25 °C to 600 °C under quasi-static loading.
At temperatures above 600 °C or under dynamic loading, additional deformation mechanisms may become important.
Mechanical-property changes should correlate with measurable increases in lattice distortion or nanoscale precipitate formation.

contradictions.description: The material is described as a single-phase solid solution but also as 'FCC/BCC,' which ordinarily denotes a two-phase state unless the intended alternative phases are clarified.

The stated boundary restricts the explanation to single-phase solid solutions, while the intervention is intended to create nanoscale precipitates and thus a heterogeneous or multiphase modified state.
